newsitem.title: UK: Mark/Swedish crown slides, other crosses steady.
newsitem.headline: Mark/Swedish crown slides, other crosses steady.

text.p: The mark slid against the Swedish crown by Europe's midsession, but was stable against other European currencies amid a lack of fresh news.
Mark/Swedish crown weakened on follow-through selling after it dropped through several technical support levels on Tuesday as sterling's strength against the mark dragged the German currency lower.

"Mark/Stockie's very much carrying on the sentiment from yesterday. Technically we're looking at 4.4950 (crowns) after hitting 4.5100 and 4.5000 on the heavy stops we saw triggered," said one trader at a Scandinavian bank in London.
The mark was at 4.5100/30 at 1104 GMT after bouncing off the session low of 4.4980. It was at 4.5350/80 in late European trade on Tuesday.
Traders said the market was unperturbed by Swedish Finance Minister Erik Asbrink's remark that Sweden's decision on participation in Europe's single currency could not run counter to public opinion.
A Sifo poll on Tuesday said 35 percent of Swedes opposed joining EMU.
Asbrink also said there would be no decision for a few weeks yet on Sweden's participation in EMU.

The market was also closely monitoring how French political parties stood in the opinion polls ahead of the May 25/June 1 National Assembly elections, after the opposition parties recently began to catch up with the ruling coalition.

A new Louis Harris poll out on Wednesday gave the centre-right coalition parties 39 percent against 28 percent for the Socialists. The mark softened to 3.3736/39 French francs from Tuesday's 3.3750/52.
The lira, meanwhile, showed little reaction to Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi's widely-expected victory in a confidence vote on the planned 1997 mini-budget late on Tuesday.
Mark/lira was at 988.60/35 against 990.70/1.00 on Tuesday.

Traders said the mark crosses were now looking to dollar/mark for direction. Dollar sentiment was dampened in European trade by a report from Japanese news agency Kyodo that Japan, the U.S. and Germany were exploring the possibility of intervening to sell dollars for yen.

"It's dependent on the dollar. With the report about apparent collusion on intervention, in the natural course of events dollar/mark would come off on that...in which case there is the chance of the mark moving up again on the crosses," said a trader at another Scandinavian bank.
Later in the day, German Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt is due to speak on the euro at 1500 GMT.
Meanwhile, new British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook was in Paris on his first trip abroad since taking office after the Labour Party's landslide win in Britain's parliamentary elections last week.

French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said on Wednesday that the latest moves by the new British government appeared to show a willingness to join EMU. Cook was due to meet his French counterpart Herve de Charette later in the day.
